why: every definition on the board refuses it, which makes it the board's negative control: a case they all decide the same way is worth nothing for separating them and everything for checking that a definition is not simply saying yes.
status_why: N. Cooke introduces it as the example of a system with NO integration, against a recurrently connected network; nothing in the seven papers treats it as a candidate.

quote: Indeed, the purportedly nonconscious protozoans and bacteria do all these things.
why: the case that splits the board. Living Mirror counts them conscious because all living systems are; self-modelling inference and EIT refuse them; IIT does not decide without a computation nobody has performed.
status_why: N by the field's default, which Cooke names as a default in the act of disputing it: 'the PURPORTEDLY NONCONSCIOUS protozoans and bacteria'. Living Mirror's whole claim is that this default is wrong, so scoring it as N is what makes the disagreement visible.

quote: The focus on internal dynamics in IIT does allow it to account for the phenomenon of dreaming, however.
why: internal dynamics continue with no external input, so every internally-defined theory counts it and the two that require environmental coupling - enactive, criticality - do not clearly rule.
status_why: P. Dreaming is treated throughout as a state to be ACCOUNTED FOR rather than argued about; Cooke credits IIT with accommodating it, which presupposes there is something there.

quote: Other authors have focused solely on states of unconsciousness during general anesthesia ( Hudetz, 2012 ), epilepsy ( Blumenfeld and Taylor, 2003 ), or sleep ( Steriade et al.
why: the clinical case the whole disorders-of-consciousness literature turns on. Living Mirror alone counts them conscious, because they are alive.
status_why: N by clinical convention, which is the convention the disorders-of-consciousness literature runs on and which wahbeh2022 cites as a state OF UNCONSCIOUSNESS.

thing: coma, vegetative state, minimally conscious state
quote: , Coma, Vegetative State/Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome, Minimally Conscious State.
why: three states the literature separates and most definitions on this board cannot: only dual-capacity and criticality attempt to grade them, and only Living Mirror gives a verdict from the definition alone.
status_why: N. farisco2018 groups them as disorders OF consciousness and the clinical question is how much residual consciousness remains, which presupposes the baseline verdict.

quote: However, even in this case, what seems plausible to model and eventually simulate is not consciousness as such, but only the cerebral configuration (i.
why: farisco2018 states the gap in its own words - what is simulated is the cerebral configuration and not consciousness as such - so every definition here refuses it and the correlational sense that would accept it is the one the paper declines to hold.
status_why: U, and deliberately. This is the question farisco2018 is asking, not a case it settles. A P or an N here would be the board inventing its own answer.

quote: As described earlier, consciousness is said to be composed of arousal as well as awareness, making meditation (a practice where awareness is increased), a sort of “super-conscious” state.
why: raised awareness with full arousal, which dual-capacity scores as MORE conscious than baseline; the paper calls it a 'super-conscious' state, which a single-axis definition has no way to represent.
status_why: P. gervais2023 describes it as a practice where awareness is INCREASED, a sort of 'super-conscious' state, which cannot be read as an absence.

quote: Even when it is interrupted by sleep or anesthesia, people experience consciousness with a certain continuity.
why: ouwersloot2020 says consciousness has continuity across sleep, so the stream-like and brain-local senses count it while the arousal-requiring one cannot.
status_why: U. ouwersloot2020 says consciousness has continuity across sleep while the dual-capacity sense requires arousal that sleep removes. The literature here genuinely splits.

quote: sensorimotor skills—is difficult for computers, and vice versa ( Moravec, 1988 ; Pinker, 1994 ; Sheikh et al.
why: Moravec's paradox as a case: the tasks a computer finds hard are the ones consciousness is said to make easy. Nothing on the board counts a computer conscious, but they refuse it for different reasons, which is what a case is for.
status_why: N by current consensus, and forti2025 uses Moravec's paradox to mark the gap rather than to argue a computer might be conscious.

thing: a person in psychedelic or shamanic state
quote: psychedelics and shamanic state of consciousness ( n = 4); delirium ( n = 1); meditative state ( n = 2).
why: intense experience with altered content, which every experience-based definition counts.
status_why: P. gervais2023 counts it among ALTERED states of consciousness, which presupposes the state is present and altered rather than absent.

quote: Although normal sleep is not considered to be a conscious state, some sleepers may experience some forms of consciousness during sleep.
why: the case that breaks a single verdict on sleep: unconscious by convention, conscious by report, in one sentence of one paper.
status_why: P, and it is the paper's own concession: normal sleep is not considered a conscious state, yet some sleepers DO experience forms of consciousness during it.

quote: During sleep, wakefulness is entirely suspended and awareness is partially, but not completely dissolved.
why: arousal gone and awareness partly present - the split dual-capacity cannot score.
status_why: U. Wakefulness entirely suspended and awareness only PARTIALLY dissolved is exactly the configuration dual-capacity was built for and cannot resolve.

thing: a behaviourally conscious patient who fails the test
quote: Significantly many behaviourally conscious patients failed the same test ( Monti et al.
why: separates a definition from its instrument. Criticality and dual-capacity ARE their tests, so they inherit the test's error; the phenomenal and inference senses do not.
status_why: P, and this is the board's sharpest case: the patient is behaviourally conscious and the instrument says otherwise.

thing: a person in hypnosis or concentrative trance
quote: consciousness occur during hypnosis and other forms of religious or concentrative trance, meditation, “peak-experiences” such as being in a flow, focused concentration and in states induced by medication, alcohol, or drugs ( Ludwig, 1966 ; Tart, 1969 , 1980 ;
why: awareness redirected rather than reduced, which nothing on the board refuses.
status_why: P. Listed by ouwersloot2020 among the states in which consciousness OCCURS, beside meditation and flow.

thing: a person in a dissociative episode
quote: We encounter psychopathology of the state of consciousness in dissociative disorders, sleep disorders, PTSDs, and conversion disorders, but also in substance-related and addictive disorders.
why: consciousness present and disordered, which is ouwersloot2020's case for defining the term clinically rather than metaphysically.
status_why: P. Named as psychopathology OF the state of consciousness, which requires the state to be present in order to be disordered.
